query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored aging treatment of single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW can induce a controlled dual‐phase microstructure with fine, ductile B2 precipitates dispersed in a continuous BCC matrix, which will enhance room-temperature ductility without compromising the high‐temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventionally or SLM‐processed single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high‐temperature mechanical performance and irradiation tolerance but poor room-temperature ductility (e.g., ~2% compressive plasticity).
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully calibrated aging heat-treatment protocol (at intermediate temperatures below the melting point, e.g., 800–1000 °C for controlled durations) to induce fine B2 precipitate formation within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature for ductility, high-temperature tests up to 1600 °C for strength assessment, and irradiation experiments (helium ion implantation and dual-beam heavy-ion irradiation up to ~8 dpa) under reactor-relevant conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a continuous BCC matrix and uniformly dispersed, nanoscale (e.g., <20 nm) ductile B2 precipitates located both intragranularly and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The precipitated B2 phase provides localized regions that are more amenable to dislocation motion and crack blunting at room temperature while simultaneously acting as sinks for irradiation-induced defects. Meanwhile, the BCC matrix retains the inherent high-temperature strength and phase stability required for elevated-temperature operation. The coherent or semi-coherent B2 precipitates help to bridge grain boundaries and limit premature failure, thus boosting ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with untreated single‐phase NbMoTaW, the aged dual‐phase alloy is expected to exhibit a substantial increase in room-temperature ductility (targeting improvements to >20% strain), retain high yield strengths at elevated temperatures (with minimal decrease, within ~20% of the original value), and maintain or even improve irradiation resistance by reducing defect accumulation through enhanced defect recombination at the precipitates.
generation.baseline: The as‐produced single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy, known to exhibit exceptional high-temperature strength and irradiation tolerance but very limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial dual-phase microstructure should remain stable at high temperatures (up to about 1600 °C) and under irradiation doses up to roughly 8 dpa with reactor-relevant helium implantation energies; outside these ranges, phase instability or coarsening may occur.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC5995863 demonstrates that microstructural engineering via phase inversion in other RHEAs can improve ductility, and PMC6427779 shows that processing routes (like SLM) can influence microstructure in refractory alloys, the application of an aging‐induced dual-phase strategy to NbMoTaW is novel. It remains uncertain whether controlled aging can reproducibly induce the desired fine B2 precipitates without forming coarse or deleterious phases, especially under conditions that also require maintaining irradiation resistance (as discussed in PMC6397024 and PMC10154406).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples: one set remaining in the as-cast single-phase BCC condition and the other subjected to the tailored aging treatment to induce B2 precipitation. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to verify the formation, size, and distribution of the B2 precipitates. Perform mechanical tests at room temperature (tensile or compressive tests) to quantify ductility, high-temperature compression/tensile tests up to 1600 °C to evaluate yield strength, and irradiation experiments (using helium implantation and dual-beam heavy-ion irradiation to ~8 dpa) followed by nanoindentation and defect density assessment.
measurements: Irradiation-induced defect density (from TEM or APT)
Nanoindentation hardness variation pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility (for instance, improvement of less than 10% absolute increase in strain) or if high-temperature strength degrades by more than ~20%, or if irradiation experiments reveal increased defect accumulation relative to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, a design methodology, based on thermodynamic calculations combined with experimental and simulation components, has been herein established for the development of promising irradiation-resistant RHEAs. Following this methodology, a quinary RHEA was designed and studied in terms of irradiation resistance, thermal stability, and strength. Such HEA shows irradiation resistance to dislocation loop and cavity formation under heavy ion irradiation and He implantation (even after 9% He implantation) with hardness values (in the annealed state) that are higher than the value in pure W. The irradiation resistance to loop and cavity formation under dual-beam and He implantation is higher than in other HEAs and pure metals studied in the literature. All results are discussed correlating the experimental results with modeling insights. We acknowledge that further work (e.g., response to neutron irradiation) is necessary to advance the technology readiness level (TRL) of this material and that the effect of composition changes in mechanical strength should be investigated. In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
